taxonomyNote: Elk (wapiti, Cervus canadensis) were long treated as the same species as red deer; genetic evidence shows they are separate species. Sources and records that file North American elk under Cervus elaphus describe elk, not red deer.
fieldMarks: Stags typically 160-240 kg and 175-250 cm long, shoulder height about 95-130 cm; hinds much smaller, 120-170 kg
Reddish-brown in summer; greyer or greyish-brown in winter, with a rump patch
Only stags carry antlers; in larger European stags the top tines form a crown or cup
Smaller than the North American elk, which was once treated as the same species
behavior: Mature animals stay in single-sex groups for most of the year
The rut runs from August into early winter; stags roar, where elk bugle, and may hold as many as 20 hinds
range: Native to most of Europe, the Caucasus, Anatolia, Iran, parts of Western Asia and the Atlas Mountains of North Africa; introduced to the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South America. In Texas it is an introduced, uncommon exotic; the Mammals of Texas says such introduced species are mostly limited to a few exotic game ranches and seldom found in free-ranging populations.

lookalikes.name: Elk
lookalikes.howToTell: Elk are larger, and their stags bugle during the rut where red deer stags roar; European red deer antlers end in a crown or cup of tines rather than the elk's throw-back top tines.
